chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Sectors Matter More Than You Think

lessons.title: Same Market, Different Rules: Why Industries Behave Differently

body.text: The Nifty 50 shows up as one number on your Zerodha screen, but it is a bundle of very different businesses. A bank, a software exporter, a cement maker, and a soap company do not earn money the same way, do not fear the same risks, and cannot be judged with the same yardstick. Before you analyse a stock, you have to know which rulebook its industry plays by.

children.text: You already know how to read a P&L and a balance sheet. The problem is that most investors then apply the same checklist to every company: low P/E is cheap, high debt is bad, fast revenue growth is good. That checklist quietly breaks the moment you move from one industry to another. This course fixes that, one sector at a time. This first lesson shows you why it has to be done at all.
What Makes One Industry Different From Another

markDefs.definition: How much money a business must invest in plants, machinery, networks, or other fixed assets to generate each rupee of revenue. Cement, steel, and telecom are capital intensive; IT services and FMCG are capital light.

children.text: Every industry can be described along five dimensions: what drives its revenue, what its biggest cost is, how much

it carries, which outside force it is most exposed to, and how tightly it is regulated. Change any one of these and the way the stock behaves changes with it. Look at four household names from the Nifty 50 through that lens.

children.text: Read across any row and you can see the problem. There is no single metric that tells you how all four are doing. A good quarter for HDFC Bank means healthy loan growth with low bad loans. A good quarter for TCS means strong deal wins and stable margins. A good quarter for UltraTech means higher volumes and fuel costs coming down. A good quarter for HUL means volume growth, not just price hikes.
Same Year, Same Market, Opposite Outcomes

These differences are not academic. They decide returns. Calendar year 2022 is the cleanest recent example. The Nifty 50 ended the year roughly flat. Underneath that calm headline, two NSE sectoral indices went in completely opposite directions.

body.context: Same country, same year, same stock exchange. The only real difference was the industry.

body.title: Why did banks and IT move in opposite directions?

children.text: The same macro event, central banks raising interest rates to fight inflation, hit the two sectors in opposite ways.

columns.label: IT services
points: US Federal Reserve hikes raised fears of a US slowdown
Clients in the US and Europe were expected to cut technology budgets
IT stocks had traded at rich valuations after 2021, so expectations of slower growth hit prices hard

columns.label: Public sector banks
points: RBI repo rate hikes let banks reprice loans upward, supporting interest margins
Years of bad loan clean-up after the 2015 Asset Quality Review had brought NPAs down sharply
Stocks had been trading at deep discounts to book value, so improving profits triggered a big rerating

body.title: What Sector Concentration Costs You
body.prompt: Riya has a ₹5,00,000 portfolio. She holds 60% of it in IT stocks because she works in tech and 'understands the industry'. The remaining 40% is spread across other sectors. Suppose her IT holdings fall 26% in a year, in line with the index, and everything else stays flat. How much money does she lose, in rupees?
body.explanation: Her IT holding is ₹5,00,000 × 60% = ₹3,00,000. A 26% fall on that is ₹3,00,000 × 26% = ₹78,000. That is a 15.6% hit to her whole portfolio in a year when the Nifty 50 was roughly flat. The loss came from sector concentration, not from bad stock picking.

children.text: Here is where most retail analysis goes wrong. Screener.in will happily show you a debt to equity ratio for HDFC Bank and for UltraTech Cement side by side. The number is calculated the same way. What it means is not.

body.title: High Leverage in a Bank vs High Leverage in a Cement Company

columns.label: Bank with borrowed funds 8x its equity
points: Deposits and borrowings are the raw material a bank lends out
8 to 10 times leverage is normal for a well-run Indian bank
The RBI sets minimum capital adequacy ratios, so the real test is capital adequacy and asset quality, not debt to equity

columns.label: Cement company with debt 8x its equity
points: Debt funds plants that earn nothing until demand shows up
Interest must be paid even when prices and volumes fall in a downturn
At this level the company would be in serious distress and facing lender pressure

children.text: The same trap applies to valuation. A P/E of 55 looks absurd next to a P/E of 8. But a steady consumer franchise with decades of predictable earnings and a cyclical commodity producer are not the same kind of asset. The market is not being irrational by pricing them differently. It is pricing different levels of growth, stability, and risk.

body.title: The 'Cheaper Stock' Argument
body.scenario: Your colleague has read that Hindustan Unilever trades at a P/E of around 55 while Coal India trades at a P/E of around 8. He says: 'Coal India is seven times cheaper. Anyone buying HUL at these levels is overpaying.'
body.prompt: What is wrong with comparing these two P/E ratios directly? What would you tell him to compare instead?
body.modelAnswer: The two companies sit in different sectors with different rules. HUL is an FMCG business with stable demand, low capital needs, and earnings that rarely fall sharply, so the market pays a high multiple for that predictability. Coal India is a government-controlled commodity producer whose earnings depend on coal prices, volumes, and policy decisions, and which faces long-term questions about the energy transition, so the market applies a low multiple. A low P/E does not automatically mean cheap. A fair comparison is HUL against other FMCG companies such as Nestle India, Dabur, or Britannia, and Coal India against its own historical P/E range and other commodity producers. Compare within a sector first, then decide whether the sector itself deserves your money.

body.title: Which Comparison Makes Sense?
body.question: You want to know whether ICICI Bank's profitability is strong. Which comparison is the most meaningful?
options: ICICI Bank's net profit margin vs Infosys's net profit margin
ICICI Bank's return on assets vs HDFC Bank's and Axis Bank's return on assets
ICICI Bank's debt to equity vs Asian Paints's debt to equity
ICICI Bank's P/E vs the Nifty 50's overall P/E
body.explanation: Banks should be compared with other banks, using metrics that fit how banks make money. Return on assets is a core profitability measure for lenders. Comparing a bank's margins or leverage with an IT or paint company tells you almost nothing, and the index P/E blends dozens of unrelated businesses.

children.text: Every Sector Has Its Own Vocabulary

Listen to any earnings call and you will notice that management in each industry talks about a different set of numbers. These sector-specific KPIs are what analysts actually track, often more closely than net profit. You will learn each of them in depth later in the course. For now, get familiar with the names.

body.title: Sector KPIs You Will Meet in This Course

cards.definition: Net Interest Margin: interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings, as a percentage of interest-earning assets. The core measure of a lender's pricing power.
Gross Non-Performing Assets: loans where interest or principal is overdue for more than 90 days, as a percentage of total loans. The headline measure of bad loans.
Total Contract Value of new deals signed in a quarter. A lead indicator of revenue over the next few years.
Growth in the number of units sold, excluding the effect of price hikes. Tells you whether demand is really growing or the company is just charging more.
Actual production as a percentage of installed capacity. High utilisation usually means pricing power; low utilisation means price wars.
The value of contracts won but not yet executed. Divided by annual revenue, it shows how many years of work are already locked in.
Average Revenue Per User per month. Since telecom networks are mostly fixed cost, every rupee of ARPU increase flows largely to profit.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Before comparing a company's ratios with another company, first check that both belong to the same ___, because the same ratio can mean very different things across industries.
body.explanation: Ratios are only comparable within a peer group that shares the same business model, cost structure, and risks. Cross-sector comparisons of raw ratios are one of the most common analysis mistakes.

body.text: Owning many stocks is not the same as being diversified. Ten IT stocks, or a portfolio of three banks, two NBFCs, and a financial services mutual fund, all respond to the same sector forces. Check your holdings on Console or in your CAMS/KFintech statement by sector, not by count.

body.title: Put a Sector Lens on Your Own Portfolio
steps: List every stock you own directly and note the sector each belongs to (Screener.in shows it on the company page)
For your equity mutual funds, open the latest monthly factsheet and note the top three sector weights
Add up your total exposure to each sector across stocks and funds combined
Flag any single sector above roughly a third of your equity money and ask whether that is a deliberate choice
For your largest sector, write down its revenue driver, biggest cost, and biggest outside sensitivity using the five dimensions from this lesson

points: Every industry has its own rulebook: a different revenue driver, cost structure, capital intensity, outside sensitivity, and regulator
The same macro event can help one sector and hurt another; in 2022, Nifty PSU Bank and Nifty IT finished nearly 100 percentage points apart
A ratio is calculated the same way for every company but means very different things across sectors; 8x leverage is normal for a bank and dangerous for a cement maker
Low P/E does not mean cheap and high P/E does not mean expensive until you compare within the same sector
Each sector has its own KPIs, such as NIM for banks, deal TCV for IT, and volume growth for FMCG, which often matter more than headline profit
Holding many stocks in the same sector is concentration, not diversification
